strengths: Clean and correct theoretical contribution: the paper derives an elegant decomposition of mutual information as a KL divergence between two reciprocal processes (joint vs. independent coupling), which via Girsanov's theorem reduces to the squared difference of diffusion drifts (Theorem 4.1). Unlike MINDE, the resulting estimator avoids the T→∞ bias term KL(q_T^A||q_T^B), which is a genuine practical advantage.

Useful generalizations are provided beyond MI: general KL divergence estimation (Thm A.1), differential entropy (A.2), pointwise mutual information (A.3), and interaction information (A.4), showing the framework's breadth.

Evaluation on established, community-recognized benchmarks (Czyż et al. 2023 low-dimensional suite; Butakov et al. image-manifold benchmarks) with ground truth, multiple seeds, and strong baselines (MINDE, MINE, InfoNCE, NWJ, D-V, KSG, DoE, MIENF, AE+WKL). Results are competitive with or better than prior generative estimators, including on the heavy-tailed Cauchy case via an asinh transform.

Honest and thorough limitations section (heavy tails, first-moment requirements of bridge matching, sample-hungry training), plus an instructive appendix (B.3) showing that a competing method's strong performance relies on inductive bias (bottleneck dimension matching intrinsic dim).
Good reproducibility: detailed architectures, hyperparameters, compute budgets, and use of official benchmark repositories.
weaknesses: Moderate novelty: the core machinery (KL between diffusions via drift differences, Eq. 7) is standard, and the contribution is largely an application of existing bridge-matching and Girsanov tools to MI estimation, closely following MINDE's template with bridges instead of score-based diffusions.

The 'unbiased estimator' claim is only valid with exact drifts; with neural drift approximations the estimator inherits approximation bias, and the paper provides no analysis (theoretical or empirical) of the variance or statistical error of the estimator, which is critical for MI estimation where high variance is a known pitfall.

The closest competitor, MINDE, is not included in the image-data benchmark (Figure 1), so the claim of being 'the best among all bias-free estimators' on image data is not directly supported against the most relevant diffusion-based baseline on that benchmark.

Image experiments use only 3 seeds and asymptotic CIs, which is thin for supporting superiority claims; low-dimensional results are essentially on par with MINDE, so the overall empirical advantage is modest.

Several presentation defects: typos and inconsistencies (e.g., 'vθ(·,0) ≈ vjoint(·)' should be vind, 'Radom-Nikodym', 'Theis type', 'alternated' for 'altered'), and Algorithm 1's pseudo-code is awkwardly interleaved with the proof of Theorem 4.1, hurting readability.
Practical applicability concerns are acknowledged but not explored: high sample requirements, fixed ϵ=1 with no ablation over volatility, and no experiments on real (non-synthetic) data.

strengths: The core theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) is clean: expressing MI as a KL between reciprocal processes and decomposing it into a difference of drifts via Girsanov/disintegration is elegant, and removing the residual bias term present in MINDE's KL(q_T^A || q_T^B) is a genuine theoretical advantage.

The practical algorithm (shared network with a binary conditional flag) is a sensible trick for making the drift-difference estimator more accurate, and the generative byproduct (learned conditional bridges) is a nice bonus.

Evaluation is reasonably broad: the standard Czyż et al. (2023) low-dimensional benchmark plus image-manifold benchmarks, with multiple seeds, matched training budgets, and honest discussion of failure on heavy-tailed (Cauchy) distributions.

The additional experiments in Appendix B.3 critically exposing the inductive bias of the AE+WKL baseline (bottleneck matched to ground-truth intrinsic dimension) are a valuable contribution to fair benchmarking.
Useful generalizations (general KL estimation, differential entropy, PMI, interaction information) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the estimator is a fairly direct transplant of the well-known Girsanov drift-difference KL decomposition (already standard in bridge matching, Schrödinger bridge, and MINDE) to reciprocal processes for MI. The delta over MINDE (Franzese et al., 2024) is essentially replacing diffusion scores with bridge drifts to remove the T→∞ bias term, which is an incremental contribution.

On the main low-dimensional benchmark the results are essentially on par with MINDE (Table 1/4); the paper's own text concedes 'the performance of our estimator is similar to that of MINDE §3'. The empirical gains beyond removing MINDE's (small) terminal bias term are not clearly demonstrated.

The 'unbiased' claim is overstated: unbiasedness holds only for exact drifts. With learned neural drifts the practical estimator carries unknown approximation bias, and the paper provides no variance or error analysis of the estimator (e.g., behavior of the 1/(1−t) drift terms near t=1, variance of the Monte Carlo estimate in Algorithm 1).

The headline claim that InfoBridge is 'the best among all bias-free estimators featured' is not rigorously supported; on the low-dimensional benchmark it is comparable to MINDE variants, and the image-benchmark comparison includes no MINDE results, weakening the direct ablation of the claimed advantage.

Several presentation issues: typos (e.g., 'vθ(·, 0) ≈ vjoint' should be vind; 'Theis type of models'), the self-referential bullet-numbering style (§4.1), and the negative-discount footnote framing of competitor setups can read as defensive rather than neutral.

Applicability restrictions inherited from bridge matching (finite first moments, high sample requirements, sensitivity to ϵ, heavy tails without ad-hoc asinh transforms) are acknowledged but not empirically explored beyond a single distribution; no ablations on ϵ or network capacity are reported.
Reproducibility is hampered: no code release is mentioned despite a method whose practical performance depends on subtleties (EMA, shared-vs-separate networks, conditioning trick).

strengths: The paper presents a clean and elegant theoretical result (Theorem 4.1) that connects mutual information estimation to the difference of drifts of reciprocal processes via the disintegration theorem and Girsanov theorem, yielding an estimator that is unbiased in theory, unlike MINDE which retains a bias term KL(q_T^A||q_T^B) that only vanishes as T→∞.

The practical algorithm (InfoBridge) is well-designed; the single-network conditional parametrization with binary input to jointly learn v_joint and v_ind is a sensible engineering choice that reduces the error from differencing two independently trained networks.

Comprehensive evaluation on the standard Czyż et al. (2023) benchmark with 10 seeds and on image-based benchmarks (Butakov et al., 2024a), showing performance comparable to MINDE on low-dimensional tasks and as good as or better than previous best methods (MIENF, AE+WKL 5-NN) on image data, while being free of their inductive biases.

Honest limitations section: the authors clearly acknowledge the inapplicability to Cauchy-type distributions and data-hungry training, and the appendix analysis of AE+WKL's brittleness with increased bottleneck dimension is a valuable and fair contribution.

Useful extensions provided: general KL divergence estimation (Theorem A.1), differential entropy estimation, pointwise MI, and interaction information, which broaden the potential impact of the framework.
Generally clear writing and logical structure, with a well-motivated positioning of the method relative to non-parametric, discriminative, and generative estimators.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: Theorem 4.1 is a relatively direct application of the known KL-between-diffusions formula (Eq. 7) to the specific case of reciprocal processes, and the overall contribution is incremental over the recent diffusion-based MI estimator MINDE (Franzese et al., 2024); the main advance is removing the T→∞ bias term, which is a somewhat narrow delta.

The 'unbiased' claim holds only for exact drifts; in practice the drifts are approximated by neural networks, so the deployed estimator is biased, and the paper provides no quantitative analysis of this approximation bias or of the estimator's variance, both of which are important for an MI estimator.

The generalizations in Appendices A.1 (general KL), A.2 (entropy), A.3 (PMI), and A.4 (interaction information) are stated theoretically but not empirically validated at all; claims about practical applicability of these extensions are unsupported.

On the low-dimensional benchmark, InfoBridge performs similarly to MINDE (the authors themselves state this), so the empirical case for the new estimator rests mainly on synthetic image benchmarks, which are limited to two distribution families (Gaussians, rectangles) at 16×16 and 32×32 with only 3 seeds and large confidence regions at high MI values.

Computational cost is significant (6–18 A100 GPU-hours per seed for 32×32 images, ~27M-parameter U-Net, 100k gradient steps) for a MI estimation task; the claim that computational complexity is 'comparable to MINDE' is asserted but not demonstrated with measurements.
The claimed real-world relevance (text-to-image alignment, self-supervised learning) is purely speculative; no experiments on any non-synthetic data are included.

Several minor issues undermine polish: typos ('Theis type', 'Radom-Nikodym', 'completely destablizes'), a suspected typo in §4.3 ('vθ(·, 0) ≈ vjoint(·)' should presumably be vind), and the asinh preprocessing for heavy-tailed cases being presented in the main results table without full clarity that it is an estimator-specific preprocessing choice in the headline comparison.

strengths: The paper presents a clean and correct theoretical contribution: the decomposition of mutual information as the KL divergence between two reciprocal processes built from Brownian bridges (Theorem 4.1), and the resulting drift-difference estimator that is unbiased in the population limit — this avoids the bias term KL(q_T^A || q_T^B) that plagues MINDE-style estimators.

The generalization in Appendix B.1 (KL divergence between arbitrary distributions via drift differences with a free reference distribution p(x0)) and the entropy estimation recipe in B.2–B.3 add value beyond the core MI estimator.

The empirical evaluation is comprehensive: a standard low-dimensional benchmark (Czyż et al.), image-based manifold benchmarks, and a real-world protein embedding benchmark (ProtTrans5, D=1024), with comparisons against a broad set of classical, discriminative, flow-based, and diffusion-based estimators.

The ablation studies are thorough: sensitivity to the volatility coefficient ε, network capacity (28k–27M parameters), and honest analysis of the inductive-bias issues in the AE+WKL baseline (Appendix C.5), plus a clearly stated limitations section (heavy tails, data requirements).
The claimed result of being the best inductive-bias-free estimator on image benchmarks is well supported, and the protein-embedding results (MAE 0.04 vs. 9.29 for MINDE-C) are striking.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate and largely incremental: the core machinery (Girsanov-based KL between diffusions with equal volatility, disintegration, conditional bridge matching) is assembled from known results in [69, 60, 88, 28], and the main step — applying KL(Q_joint || Q_ind) — is a natural combination of MINDE's idea with diffusion bridge matching rather than a fundamentally new technique.

The 'unbiased estimator' claim is overstated: unbiasedness holds only when the drifts are known exactly. In practice both drifts are approximated by a single neural network, and the estimator involves a squared difference of two learned functions, so approximation error propagates nonlinearly into the estimate. No theoretical analysis of approximation/variance error is provided, and the heuristic justification of the shared-network trick (§4.2) is empirical only.

The method inherits the bridge-matching requirement of a finite first moment, which visibly fails on Cauchy-type data (Table 1), and the remedy (asinh tail-shortening transform) is applied selectively, which complicates the 'one method, no preprocessing' narrative.

Some comparisons may flatter the method: MINDE runs (2–5 GPU-hours) are substantially cheaper than InfoBridge (6–18 GPU-hours per seed), and only 3 seeds are used for the main method versus 5–10 for competitors, with ablation configurations mostly run once; the cost/robustness trade-off is not fully analyzed.

Writing and presentation issues: several typos ('Euler-Maryama', 'skews the comparison', 'Rœlly'), broken cross-references in the parse (M2, M4.1 style placeholders), and Table 1/9 are dense and hard to read in the current format.

Significance for real applications is plausible but not yet demonstrated: the only real-data experiment is a semi-synthetic benchmark built from class labels of protein embeddings; no application to the settings the discussion invokes (e.g., self-supervised learning or text-to-image alignment) is included.

strengths: The theoretical construction is clean and self-contained: the decomposition of mutual information into a time-integral of squared drift differences between reciprocal processes (Theorem 4.1) is derived rigorously via disintegration and Girsanov, and the generalization to arbitrary KL divergence (Theorem B.1) and differential entropy (Appendix B.2) is a nice bonus.

The paper uses well-established, standard benchmarks (Czyz et al. NeurIPS 2023; image manifold benchmarks; the ProtTrans5 protein embedding benchmark), enabling direct comparison with a broad set of baselines including MINDE, MIENF, flows, and classical estimators.

The protein embedding experiments (1024-d, real-world data) are a genuinely useful addition beyond synthetic benchmarks, where the method shows a large margin over MINDE (MAE 0.04 vs 9.29) and classical estimators.

The ablation on the volatility coefficient and the shared-network-with-binary-conditioning design choice are sensible, and the honest discussion of the failure case (Cauchy distribution) and limitations of the bridge-matching framework is appreciated.
The single-network parametrization for the two drifts, motivated by error cancellation in the drift difference, is a practical and empirically supported design decision.
weaknesses: Limited novelty relative to MINDE (Franzese et al., ICLR 2024): the core idea — KL between distributions equals the time-integral of squared differences between learned drifts of two stochastic processes — is the same structural result, merely transplanted from backward diffusions to Brownian-bridge mixtures. The bridge-matching machinery itself is taken nearly wholesale from prior work (Zhou et al. 2024; Shi et al. 2023). This reads as an incremental variant of an existing diffusion-based MI estimator rather than a new methodology.

The headline claim of an 'unbiased estimator' is overstated. Unbiasedness holds only if the drifts vjoint and vind are learned exactly; in practice neural approximation error, and the fact that the estimator integrates squared differences of approximate drifts, introduces bias that is never quantified or bounded. This is precisely the criticism the paper levels against direct PDF-estimation approaches in Related Work.

The claimed superiority on image benchmarks does not hold up: in Table 6, AE+WKL with inductive bias (MAE 0.26) and MIENF (0.45) outperform InfoBridge (0.38), so the practical 'best method' claim must be qualified as 'best among inductive-bias-free estimators.' While the fairness argument about competing methods using priors is reasonable, it weakens the significance of the empirical gains, which over MINDE-C (0.56) are moderate.

Ablation studies (Tables 2–4, Figure 3, Figure 5) are run with a single seed, and MI measurements are averaged over the last 5 training measurements rather than independent replications, so the reported stability of these results is not statistically supported. The main image benchmark also uses only 3 seeds with wide confidence intervals.

Computational cost is substantial (6–18 GPU-hours per seed for image benchmarks, plus drift training for every MI estimation task) and the claim of 'comparable computational complexity to MINDE' is asserted rather than demonstrated with measurements. The method offers no clear efficiency advantage over MINDE while being comparable or worse on several benchmarks.

Scalability claims ('paves the way for MI estimation in high dimensions') are not supported by any experiments on genuinely high-dimensional natural data; 1024-d embeddings and 32x32 synthetic images are still far from realistic use cases such as the text-to-image alignment applications cited in the discussion.

Presentation quality is below the bar for a top-tier venue: numerous typos ('Euler-Maryama', 'less then', 'that is requires of a lot of data samples'), broken cross-references in the rendered PDF (internal sections rendered as 'M4.1', 'M2'), incomplete text in the proof of Theorem B.1, empty repository URLs in Appendix C, a duplicated reference ([10]/[11]), and a reliance on unpublished lecture notes [43] for Theorem B.2.

The theoretical framing inherits rather than creates insight: the key fact that the Brownian bridge conditional drift is (x1-xt)/(1-t) is textbook material, and the mixture-of-bridges construction for the independent coupling is a straightforward application of existing bridge-matching theory to the specific KL objective.

strengths: Clean and well-motivated theoretical contribution: Theorem 4.1 expresses mutual information as the KL divergence between reciprocal processes (mixtures of Brownian bridges) and decomposes it into an integral of squared drift differences, yielding an estimator that is unbiased in principle, in contrast to diffusion-based competitor MINDE which retains a bias term KL(q_T^A || q_T^B) that only vanishes as T → ∞.

Practical algorithm is simple and well designed: the two drifts (joint and independent) are learned by conditional bridge matching and unified in a single network with a binary conditioning input, which the authors motivate plausibly (shared approximation error cancels in the difference); Algorithm 1/2 are clear and reproducible.

Comprehensive evaluation across three regimes: the Czyz et al. low-dimensional benchmark (including heavy-tailed and manifold-embedded cases), the image-based manifold benchmarks of Butakov et al. at two resolutions, and a real-world protein language model embedding task (ProtTrans5, 1024-dim) with an analytically tractable MI construction.

The paper is honest and careful in comparisons: it explicitly discusses the inductive biases of competing methods (MIENF's gaussianizability assumption, AE+WKL's bottleneck matched to intrinsic dimensionality) and includes an additional experiment (Appendix C.5, Figure 5) showing AE+WKL degrades when that bias is removed, supporting the claim that InfoBridge is the best inductive-bias-free estimator.

Useful generalizations are provided: unbiased KL divergence estimation between arbitrary distributions (Theorem B.1, with proof), differential entropy estimation via exponential-family references, and interaction information; ablations cover volatility coefficient ε, network capacity, and limitations (heavy tails, sample requirements) are discussed in a dedicated appendix.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core result follows from combining known ingredients — the Girsanov-based KL between diffusions (eq. 6) and the fact that both reciprocal processes share the same conditional bridge — and the proof of Theorem 4.1 is short. The contribution is more a new instantiation of existing bridge-matching machinery than a fundamentally new tool.

The 'unbiased estimator' claim is contingent on exactly known drifts v_joint and v_ind; in practice the drifts are learned by regression with approximation error, and the paper provides no analysis or quantification of the resulting bias/variance of the Monte Carlo estimator (e.g., no variance estimates, no convergence study in number of training steps or samples).

Performance on the low-dimensional benchmark is only comparable to MINDE (not clearly better), so the empirical advantage is mainly demonstrated on image manifolds and protein embeddings, which narrows the scope of the claimed superiority.

Method appears more computationally expensive than the closest competitor: 6–18 GPU-hours per run on A100 vs. 2–5 GPU-hours for MINDE with matched architecture, which is not analyzed or discussed as a trade-off.

Sensitivity to the volatility coefficient ε is noticeable (Table 2: MAE ranges 1.53 to 6.45; Table 3: 0.04 to 0.775), the optimal ε differs between setups, and the single-network conditioning trick is justified only empirically/heuristically; guidance on choosing ε for new data is limited.

Known failure modes (distributions without first moment, e.g., Cauchy, requiring an asinh preprocessing fix; high data requirements) restrict applicability, and the discussion of when the asinh transform is safe is brief.

Minor presentation issues: several repository URLs referenced in the appendix appear empty/broken in the manuscript, occasional typos ('then' vs 'than', 'Euler-Maryama'), and cross-references to equation/problem numbers (e.g., 'Problem (2)') are inconsistent in places.
